I/O Vision: Designing a Computer Vision Platform for Industrial Plants

How a focused product replaced a buried feature — and gave operations leaders a real pair of eyes on the floor.

Some environments simply weren’t built for human eyes.

A 200-meter conveyor in a steel plant. A chemical reactor zone where a five-minute walk takes thirty minutes of suiting up. A high-bay warehouse where a single supervisor can’t physically be everywhere at once. These are the places where computer vision earns its keep — not as a novelty, but as the only practical way to see.

I/O Vision is the platform I designed to make that seeing usable.

Who it’s for

I/O Vision was built for plant managers, floor supervisors, and CXOs running large manufacturing operations. People accountable for three things at once: safety, quality, and SOP compliance.

Their job is to know — in real time — whether a worker stepped into a restricted zone, whether a part came off the line within tolerance, whether a checklist actually got followed. Before I/O Vision, the answer to all three was usually some mix of paperwork, second-hand reports, and luck.

The problem worth solving

Vision-based use cases weren’t new. They had been quietly running inside our existing platform for years — but as a feature, not a product. Bundled inside a legacy architecture designed for sensor data, IoT telemetry, and traditional dashboards, vision was always the awkward guest at the table.

The constraints showed up everywhere:

  • The architecture wasn’t designed for video streams, so playback was sluggish and context-switching was painful.
  • The UI patterns were borrowed from numeric dashboards. Cameras don’t behave like sensors. Treating them the same flattened the experience.
  • Advanced features — multi-camera correlation, algorithm overlays, timeline scrubbing — were either hacked in or simply not possible.
  • Customers asking specifically for “a vision platform” were getting a generic IoT product with cameras attached.

The signal was loud: vision deserved its own surface.

The opportunity

The brief, in a sentence: build a dedicated platform that turns cameras into a system of record for safety, quality, and SOPs.

Not a feature. Not a module. A product.

That reframing changed everything downstream — information architecture, navigation, the visual language, the way time is represented, the way live status is communicated. Once vision was the main character, the design could finally serve it properly.

Approach: design system before screens

The temptation in any greenfield product is to start with screens — sketch the dashboard, then the detail page, then the settings. I deliberately resisted that.

Before designing a single feature, I built the design system. Foundations first: type scale, spacing rhythm, color tokens, iconography, status states, motion principles. Then the components: camera tiles, timeline rails, map markers, alert chips, status pills, layout shells.

Two reasons:

1. Vision UIs are dense. A camera view at full bleed, an event timeline beneath it, alert chips, controls, metadata, an algorithm overlay — that’s a lot of competing signals. Without a strict system, every screen becomes a fresh negotiation between elements. With one, the screens almost design themselves.

2. The platform had to scale. I/O Vision wasn’t going to ship as three screens and stop. Future modules, customer-specific views, new algorithm types — all of it needed a foundation that could absorb growth without fragmenting.

By the time I started on actual screens, every component already had a home, a behavior, and a reason to exist.

The three core experiences

I/O Vision is built around three primary surfaces, each answering a different question a plant operator asks throughout the day.

1. Camera View — “What is happening, and what just happened?”

The Camera View is where most users spend their time. A live feed of a single camera, paired with a timeline rail that lets you scrub backward through events the system has detected — a violation, a quality flag, a missed SOP step.

The design choice that mattered most here was treating the timeline as a first-class citizen, not a footer. In legacy tools, video playback controls were an afterthought tucked under the player. I pulled the timeline out and gave it room to breathe — color-coded event markers, density-aware scrubbing, jump-to-event interactions. The result: a supervisor can investigate a 12-hour shift in under a minute.

2. Map View — “Where is everything, and is anything wrong right now?”

When you’re running a plant with 80, 200, sometimes 500 cameras, a list view stops being useful around camera number 12. The Map View lays cameras out spatially — on a floor plan, a site map, a multi-building layout — and pushes live status to the surface. Online, offline, alerting, processing.

The design challenge was restraint. A map full of pulsing red dots, animated overlays, and competing labels reads as chaos, not information. I leaned hard on a quiet visual baseline — muted plan rendering, minimal markers — so that when something does need attention, it actually stands out. Status earns its color; nothing else competes for it.

3. Smart View — “How do I make my existing cameras smarter?”

Smart View is the most strategically important surface. It lets users assign algorithms — PPE detection, intrusion zones, line-crossing, object counting, SOP step verification — to cameras they already have. No new hardware. No procurement cycle. Just a configuration flow.

This was the screen that justified the whole platform commercially. It turned cameras from passive recording devices into active sensors. From a design standpoint, the work was making algorithm configuration feel like a five-minute task instead of an IT project — clear inputs, sensible defaults, visual previews of detection zones drawn directly on the camera frame.

The design philosophy: less clutter, more flow

Industrial software has a well-earned reputation for being ugly. Dense menus, twelve-color palettes, modal stacks, settings buried four levels deep. I wanted I/O Vision to feel like a piece of consumer software that happened to live in a control room.

A few principles guided that:

Navigation as muscle memory. A consistent left rail, predictable hierarchy, and a small number of top-level destinations. Users shouldn’t have to think about where something is — only what they’re looking for.

One job per screen. Camera View shows a camera. Map View shows a map. Smart View configures intelligence. Each surface refuses to be everything; together they cover everything.

Visual quiet. Generous whitespace, restrained color, type doing more work than chrome. Status and alerts get the loud colors. Everything else gets out of the way.

Motion that means something. Transitions reinforce spatial relationships — drilling from a map into a camera, from a camera into an event. No decorative animation; every motion has a job.

What the platform delivers

The most concrete outcome is structural: I/O Vision exists as a product in its own right. Customers asking for a vision platform now get a vision platform — not a sensor dashboard with cameras awkwardly stitched in.

For the operators using it, three shifts stand out:

Investigation collapses from hours to minutes. What used to take a supervisor a phone call, a walk, and a paperwork trail now takes a scrub through a timeline.

Coverage expands without adding headcount. A single operator can monitor a footprint that previously needed multiple sets of eyes — and crucially, can monitor zones where placing a human would be unsafe or impractical.

Vision becomes proactive instead of forensic. Before, footage was something you reviewed after an incident. With Smart View, the same cameras flag issues as they happen — or before.

What I’d carry forward

Two lessons from this project that I’ll apply to anything I design next:

Build the system before you build the screens. Especially in dense, multi-surface products, design system work isn’t overhead — it’s the thing that makes the rest of the design possible. Every hour spent on tokens and components saved a day of cleanup later.

Reframe the product before you redesign the UI. The biggest unlock on I/O Vision wasn’t a clever interaction or a beautiful screen. It was the decision to stop treating vision as a feature inside a bigger product, and start treating it as a product of its own. The UI followed naturally from that.

Cameras have been on factory floors for decades. What they were missing wasn’t more pixels or smarter algorithms — it was a product designed to actually use them.

I/O Vision is my attempt at that product.

https://medium.com/@akashgohil.connect/i.title: I Was Waiting for My Designs to Ship. So I Stopped Waiting and Started Coding.
https://medium.com/@akashgohil.connect/i.content:
I’m a product designer. I got tired of the two-sprint lag between a Teams handoff and a deployed component. So I built our entire design system in code myself — with Claude Code, Figma MCP, and Storybook. Here’s the workflow, the outcomes, and the part nobody talks about.

For years my workflow was the same. Design in Figma. Book a Teams handoff. Walk an engineer through the file on screen-share. File a ClickUp ticket. Wait.

Two sprints later — sometimes three — the work would ship. By then the context from the handoff meeting had evaporated. Priorities had shifted. The product manager was already asking about the next thing. And the design itself felt slightly stale, because the world had moved on while my Figma file sat in a backlog.

The shipped version was usually 80% right and 100% off. Padding subtly different. A hover state that had drifted. The focus ring I’d obsessed over quietly replaced with a default browser outline. Nothing catastrophic. Just the slow erosion of intent that happens when an idea waits four weeks in a queue.

I used to think the problem was communication. Better Teams handoffs. More detailed ClickUp tickets. Tighter Loom videos. After a few years of trying every variation, I stopped believing that.

The problem wasn’t communication. The problem was the wait itself. The design was finished on Tuesday. The code shipped a month later. Everything bad happened in the gap.

I couldn’t make engineers go faster — they had their own roadmap, their own priorities, their own backlog. So I stopped trying. I picked up the work myself.

This is the story of what that looks like in 2026, with the tooling we have now.

The shift

The first time I opened a real frontend codebase wasn’t elegant. I broke a build within an hour. I had no idea what a tsconfig was. I asked an engineer what forwardRef meant and got a five-minute answer I understood about 30% of.

But something clicked.

Once you’ve watched a Button component render from props you wrote, the gap between Figma and production starts to feel artificial. The variants you spent three days organizing into a well-named structure? They map almost 1:1 to a TypeScript prop type. The tokens you defined? They’re just CSS variables waiting to be referenced. The “states” page in your Figma file? That’s a Storybook story.

The translation layer I’d been treating as someone else’s job turned out to be the most interesting design problem in the room.

I’m still a designer. I still care more about a 2px shift in the dropdown’s position than is reasonable. But the loop between deciding something and shipping it has collapsed from weeks to hours, and that changes what I’m willing to attempt.

The pipeline

Five tools, doing one job each:

  1. Figma — where the component is designed, with explicit props in mind.
  2. Figma MCP server — exposes the Figma file as a tool an AI agent can read. Selection, properties, tokens, variants, all queryable.
  3. Figma Console MCP — the inspector layer. Lets the agent introspect what’s actually rendering, not just what was authored.
  4. Claude Code — the agent that reads the design, writes the component, wires up the story, and opens the PR.
  5. GitHub — version control and the substrate for review. Engineers see the diff like any other PR.

Storybook sits at the end of the chain as the documentation surface. The MCP server I built sits in front of the whole thing. More on that.

1. Design in Figma — but with props in mind

The biggest mindset shift is treating a Figma component as a function signature, not a picture.

Before I draw anything, I write down what props this thing should take. A button has variant, size, iconLeft, iconRight, loading, disabled. A card has media, title, body, footer, interactive. The Figma variants exist to exhaust those props, not to look pretty in a grid.

The downstream effect: when Claude Code reads the Figma component, the prop interface is sitting right there in the variant axes. There’s nothing to invent.

2. Hook up both MCPs

The first MCP — Figma’s official server — lets the agent read the file. The second — Figma Console MCP — is the inspector. Together they give two views: what the designer authored, and what is actually rendering on the canvas.

If you’ve only ever used the official MCP, install the console one too. The number of times I’ve had Claude generate a component that “looks right” except for one mystery padding value — and then fixed it instantly by letting it inspect the actual rendered tree — is high.

3. Generate the component with Claude Code

In a Claude Code session, pointed at the design system repo, I’ll ask something like:

Read the selected Figma component. Generate a TypeScript React component matching its prop variants. Use the existing tokens in src/tokens. Match the file structure in src/components/Button for consistency. Add a Storybook MDX file with one story per variant. Run the linter and fix any issues.

That’s it. Claude reads the Figma node, pulls the tokens, generates the component, scaffolds the story, runs the linter, and shows me the diff. I review it like any pull request.

The trick that makes this actually work is consistency. Every component in the repo follows the same file structure: Component.tsx, Component.stories.mdx, Component.test.tsx, index.ts. Once one component exists, the agent has a template to follow for every subsequent one. The first component is the hardest. The hundredth is fifteen minutes.

4. Inspect and test with engineers

This is the step a lot of “AI builds your design system” demos skip, and it’s the one that actually matters.

Before the component lands on main, an engineer reviews the PR. Sometimes they catch accessibility issues I missed — focus traps, ARIA roles, keyboard handlers. Sometimes they refactor for performance. Sometimes they push back on the API I designed for the prop interface, and they're right.

The reason this works smoothly — and didn’t, when handoffs happened in Teams meetings — is that the conversation is happening on real code, in PR review. Engineers can run it, poke at it, write a test against it. The feedback loop is tight and the disagreements are concrete. There’s no screen-share where I’m describing a hover state in words. They can just hover.

5. Storybook, live

Storybook is the human-facing surface. Every story is auto-deployed via Vercel on merge. Designers and engineers who don’t want to query an MCP just open the URL and browse.

Crucially, Storybook isn’t the source of truth. It’s a view. The source of truth is the code. Storybook just renders it nicely with prop controls, accessibility checks, and visual regression tests baked in.

6. Iterate

The reason this whole pipeline matters is that it makes iteration cheap. Find a bug? Edit the Figma variant, re-run Claude Code with a focused prompt, get a focused PR. Tokens drift? Run the agent against the token file and the Figma styles together. Need a new size variant of an existing component? Ten-minute change, not a sprint.

The first version of the design system took weeks. Maintaining it takes hours per week.

The piece that compounds: the MCP server

Once the design system was real, I put an MCP server in front of it. This is the part I think will matter most over the next few years.

If you strip away the marketing, a design system is a structured set of facts: a list of color tokens, a list of typography styles, a list of components with known props, a set of usage rules. That’s a database. With docs.

Most teams expose this database as a Storybook site, a Figma library, and a Notion page (or in our case, a ClickUp doc). Three or four surfaces, all manually maintained, all subtly out of sync.

An MCP server is one more surface — but it’s the one your tools can read.

What changes when AI can query the system

Engineers stop guessing imports. “Give me the import path and prop signature for the Card component” returns a verified, current answer. Not the answer from a ClickUp doc that hasn’t been updated in three months.

Token consistency improves automatically. When an engineer asks Cursor “what’s the right color for a warning background,” it reads the MCP and returns tokens.color.warning.background instead of inventing a hex. The system enforces itself.

Designers prototype faster in code. I can ask Claude “build a settings page using only components from our system” and have it actually obey, because the component list is queryable, not just documented in prose.

AI-generated UI gets on-brand by default. This one is the most underrated. As more code gets written by agents — Cursor, Claude Code, whatever comes next — the default output drifts toward generic Tailwind. An MCP-exposed design system pulls that drift back to brand. The agent reaches for your Card before it reaches for a generic div with rounded-lg shadow-md.

How it’s built

The server itself is small. It exposes a handful of tools: list_components, get_component, list_tokens, search, get_usage_examples. The data backing each one comes from the same source as Storybook: the actual component code, plus MDX files. There's no separate "MCP data store" to maintain.

This is the part I’d push hardest if you build something similar: don’t let your MCP server become another surface to maintain. Generate it from the code, the same way you generate Storybook. Otherwise you’re back to several out-of-sync surfaces, just with one more.

Outcomes

What actually changed once the pipeline was running:

  • Design-to-production time collapsed from sprints to a single afternoon for a typical component. The two-sprint wait — the thing that started this whole experiment — is gone.
  • Teams handoff meetings disappeared from my calendar. I haven’t done a screen-share design walkthrough in months. The Figma file is the prop interface; the PR is the spec; the conversation happens in PR review.
  • ClickUp tickets stopped piling up. Components don’t sit in a backlog anymore because nobody else is the bottleneck for shipping them.
  • One designer covers the whole system. Tokens, components, stories, docs, the MCP server — all maintained by me, with engineer review on every PR.
  • Token consistency is enforced, not policed. Hardcoded hex values used to slip into the codebase constantly. Now the linter catches them and the MCP server makes the right tokens easy to find, so they rarely get written in the first place.
  • AI agents across the company ship on-brand UI by default. Anyone using Cursor, Claude Code, or Claude in the IDE gets our components and tokens served to them. They don’t have to know the system — the system is in their context window.
  • Engineers spend their review time on real things. Accessibility, performance, API design. Not “this padding is 14px, should be 16px.” That part is solved.
  • Onboarding got cheap. A new hire can ask the MCP “what components exist?” and get an answer. They don’t need to memorize the library or hunt through ClickUp.

The compounding effect is the part I didn’t expect. Every component I add isn’t just a thing humans can use — it’s a thing every AI agent in the company can use. The leverage of one well-instrumented design system, in 2026, is much higher than it was even a year ago.

The things that surprised me

A few that didn’t fit cleanly above:

File structure conventions are load-bearing. The single biggest thing that made Claude Code reliable wasn’t the prompt — it was having a rigid, predictable file structure. The agent learns the pattern from one example and replicates it.

You can’t skip review. AI agents will confidently generate components with subtle accessibility bugs. Engineer review catches these. Skipping it because the demo looked good is how you ship a button that traps focus.

Start with tokens, not components. I started with a Button, because Button is the canonical first design-system component. But Button references colors, spacing, typography, radius, and motion tokens — none of which existed yet. I ended up retrofitting the token system around the Button, which is backwards. Build the tokens first.

My Figma files got worse for a while. When you start thinking in components and props, you stop wanting to draw fifty variants by hand. You start wanting to generate them. Your Figma files become more like blueprints and less like polished portfolios. Recruiters who skim Dribbble do not love this. Worth it anyway.

The takeaway

A design system used to compound by adoption: the more teams used it, the more valuable it got. That’s still true.

But now it compounds by machine-readability too. Every component I add isn’t just a thing humans use — it’s a thing every AI agent in the company uses. Every token isn’t just a CSS variable — it’s a fact in a queryable database that influences every generated UI from now on.

Product designer to design engineer isn’t really about learning to code. It’s about realising that the wait between design and production was never inevitable — it was just nobody’s job to close. So you close it.

I stopped waiting for sprints to end. I stopped booking handoff calls. The work ships on the day it’s designed.

https://medium.com/@akashgohil.connect/d.title: Designing the Faclon Labs Design System: A Foundation for Modern Industrial Software
https://medium.com/@akashgohil.connect/d.content:
How a single, opinionated system replaced years of one-off components — and finally closed the gap between design and development.

Most design systems get built after the fact.

A product ships, then a second one, then a third. Somewhere around the fourth, a designer notices that there are now five different button styles, three flavors of input field, and a color palette that’s expanded to forty-something hex values nobody remembers approving. A document gets created. It gets called a design system. It mostly describes what already exists.

That’s not the system I wanted to build for Faclon Labs.

The Faclon Labs Design System was built deliberately, before the next wave of products — as the foundation everything modern would be built on.

Why a system was non-negotiable

Faclon’s software portfolio had grown the way most industrial software grows: organically, product by product, problem by problem. Each new build started with good intentions and ended with custom components — buttons, modals, tables, form fields — drawn fresh because nothing reusable existed.

The cost of that showed up in three places:

No modern baseline. New products had nowhere to start. Every greenfield project began with a week of “what should a button look like in 2025?” — a question that should have been answered exactly once, in exactly one place.

Inconsistent results. Custom components meant custom decisions, made under custom deadlines, by whoever was on the project that quarter. The output worked, but two products from the same company looked like they came from two different companies.

A widening design-to-dev gap. Designers handed off Figma files. Developers rebuilt them from scratch in React. Pixels drifted. Spacing rounded itself. Edge cases got reinterpreted. Every handoff became a small translation layer where intent leaked out.

The fix wasn’t more documentation. It was a real system — one that designers and developers shared as a single source of truth, not two parallel artifacts pretending to match.

Scope: foundations first, components second

I designed the system in two clear layers, in that order.

Layer 1 — Foundations

This was the part that couldn’t be rushed. Foundations are the grammar of the system; if they’re wrong, everything built on top is wrong by the same amount.

Primitive tokens. The raw values — every color, every spacing step, every type size, every elevation depth. Named neutrally, scaled mathematically, deliberately decoupled from any specific use.

Semantic tokens. The meaningful layer above primitives — surface/background, text/primary, border/subtle, status/critical. Components consume these, never the primitives directly. This is the layer that lets you flip light to dark mode, or theme an entire product, without touching a single component.

Type scale. A constrained set of styles, each with a job — display, heading, body, label, caption — each tied to a token. No arbitrary type sizes. No “make this 15px just here.”

Spacing. A single rhythm running through the entire system. Every gap, every padding, every margin pulled from the same scale.

Elevation. Layered shadow tokens for depth — surfaces, popovers, modals, overlays — defined once and reused everywhere.

Light and dark mode. Built into the token architecture from day one, not bolted on later. Dark mode in industrial software isn’t a nice-to-have; control rooms, plant offices, and night shifts all need it.

Layer 2 — Components

On top of the foundations, 47 components — covering the surface area of a real product, not a marketing site. Buttons, inputs, selects, tables, tabs, modals, popovers, toasts, navigation rails, cards, chips, badges, breadcrumbs, empty states, loaders, and the rest of the working library a React product actually consumes.

Each component was built with three properties in mind:

  1. Token-driven. No hardcoded values anywhere. Every color, spacing, and radius pulled from the semantic layer.
  2. Variant-rich, but constrained. Enough flexibility to handle real product needs (sizes, states, intents) without becoming a configuration playground.
  3. Mirrored in Figma and React. Same name, same props, same behavior. What designers compose, developers can ship.

Built in Figma the way developers think

The single most important decision I made was treating the Figma library not as a sticker sheet, but as a working component system — with properties, variants, and states modeled the same way they exist in code.

Every component had its props built in:

  • A button isn’t five buttons. It’s one component with variant, size, state, and icon properties.
  • A table cell knows whether it’s a header, a body, a numeric, or an action cell — through props, not duplicates.
  • Light and dark aren’t separate libraries. They’re a mode switch on the same components.

The reason this matters: when a designer’s Figma file mirrors the structure of the React code, handoff stops being translation. A developer reading the file isn’t reverse-engineering visual decisions — they’re reading a spec. The gap between “what was designed” and “what got built” collapses to almost nothing.

This is the part of design system work that doesn’t show up in screenshots, and it’s the part that actually moves the needle.

Scoped intentionally — not a system trying to be everything

One decision I want to be explicit about: this design system is purpose-built for React-based products in the Faclon Labs portfolio. It powers I/O Vision, I/O Sense, and the modern operational software in that family.

Newer agentic products in the company — Aura and Bruce — run on a separate design system tuned for their distinct interaction model. That’s deliberate. A design system that tries to serve every possible product ends up serving none of them well. By scoping this one tightly to a coherent product family with shared patterns (data-dense dashboards, monitoring surfaces, configuration flows), every decision could be sharper.

A focused system beats a universal one. Always.

What it replaced

The most measurable shift the system delivered is a quiet one: the old design language stopped getting used.

For years, new features were built by reaching into the legacy library — older components, older tokens, older patterns that had accumulated their own debt. The moment the new system reached coverage, that pull stopped. New work went to the new library by default. Older products started getting migrated piece by piece. The design language of Faclon’s modern software unified, not because anyone mandated it, but because the new system was simply the path of least resistance.

That’s the test of a real design system. Not whether it exists, but whether teams reach for it without being asked.

The design–development relationship, rebuilt

The deeper outcome was relational.

Before the system, design and development operated like two departments separated by a translation layer. Figma files went one way. Code came back the other way. Discrepancies were normal; alignment was the exception.

After the system, the same components — same names, same variants, same tokens — exist on both sides. A designer drops a Button/primary/medium into a frame; a developer imports <Button variant="primary" size="md" />. The two artifacts aren't translations of each other. They're the same thing, expressed in two formats.

That changes how teams work. Reviews stop being about pixel discrepancies and start being about product decisions. Handoff stops being a phase and starts being continuous. New designers and developers ramp up against the same source of truth.

What I’d carry forward

Two principles from this project that I’ll apply to every design system I build next:

Tokens are the product. Components are the packaging. The instinct is to start with components — they’re visible, they’re tangible, they fill a Figma page nicely. But components are downstream. The architecture that decides whether your system can scale, theme, support new modes, and survive five years of product change lives in the token layer. Get tokens right, and components almost design themselves. Get them wrong, and no amount of component polish will save you.

A design system is infrastructure, not deliverable. You don’t ship a design system the way you ship a feature. You stand it up, then you maintain it, then you grow it. The work doesn’t end at v1. It begins there. Treating it as infrastructure — owned, versioned, governed — is the difference between a system that compounds in value and one that quietly rots into a Figma file nobody opens anymore.

A design system isn’t a deliverable. It’s the floor every future product gets to stand on.

Designed and built solo in Figma — from variables and tokens to fully propertied, production-ready components.
